job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Jade Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up early for prayer, then go to my master's classes in accounting and finance in Leicester. Afternoons I'm either in the library or behind the till at a shop in the city centre, about 16 hours a week. In the evenings I help my mother with her alteration work, hemming trousers and taking in dresses, because she has more orders than she has hours.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about how you got here.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did an accounting bachelor's at the same university and passed with an average result. No internship, because every firm that offered one wanted a connection I didn't have, and I couldn't afford to work for free anyway. I owe about 39,000 pounds. My mother sews and my father passed away some years ago, so there's no one to pay my way. I believe in earning things properly, but I'd like someone to give me the chance to earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because hard work should still count for something. I'd say it quietly at the shop, and at our community centre where people worry about their children's futures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it doesn't change much, and that's the difficulty. There are few accounting posts around Leicester for someone with my marks and no experience. I owe 39,000 pounds, and a plain year of nothing new is still a hard year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, enrol on the professional accountancy exams one paper at a time, and ask every small firm in the area whether they take trainees. I'd do 30 visits in person, with my CV on paper. I'd keep the till job and not take any new risks until I have a post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense. It's patience wearing thin, like a rope that's held a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd like someone to give you the chance. Who might do that, in your area?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small firms owned by people in my community, maybe. A face counts for more than an online form, so I'd knock on doors. I'd ask my uncle's friend who runs a tax practice for even a month's trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your mother say about the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother says to be patient and trust that things will work out, and that she'll pray for me. She also says to marry well, which is a conversation I'm not ready for. She can't pay, but her faith gives me strength.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people have always found a way, and we shouldn't wait for handouts. I'd also say firms owe it to young people to train them, and they should keep apprenticeships going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm afraid. The first jobs for an accountant are checking and entering, and software does that now. With no internship and no one to speak for me, I'd be the last in line when a firm cuts its intake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to find a firm that still trains by apprenticeship, even if it pays little. I'd ask my uncle's friend and the mosque committee for introductions. I'd also have to learn at least one software package, but only if a firm showed it to me. I'd take any trainee post and live on the till wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and a bit proud. I don't like being afraid and I won't show it at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks in a junior accountant's day would go to software first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Entering invoices, checking figures, preparing standard returns. What's left is advising clients and signing off, and no firm gives that to a newcomer without years of trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you not be willing to do to keep up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't do anything dishonest or lean on charity if I could earn. But I'd accept an apprenticeship at lower pay for three years, if it came with a recognised qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that we must hold together as families and communities, and that those with the tools should use them with some care for the rest of us. I wouldn't ask for charity, but I'd ask for time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my degree would be worth nothing. Accounting is thinking work and thinking work is the first thing to go. I'd be 26 with a 39,000 pound loan and no craft in my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the professional exams, since the fees would be wasted. I'd look for anything hands-on, like helping my mother grow her sewing into a proper tailor's shop, which robots won't do for about three more years. And I'd ask my community for any work on offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd pray more and sleep less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mother that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mother that I'm grateful for all her sewing. I'd work next to my mother as a tailor if it comes to that, because there's no shame in a trade. She'd say I was right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is responsible for helping people in those two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Families first, then the community, then the government as a last backstop. I don't like being dependent, but if the work goes everywhere, the state must help people eat and keep a roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if we don't waste it, and people should work harder and save. I'd say governments should support apprenticeships so young people have something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be scared, but with some control. Five years is a first job, some training, and a good chunk of the loan paid. I'd be 29, perhaps married, and I'd need a job that's still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any trainee post in the next year, finish the professional exams, and pay 250 a month to the loan. I'd also learn a trade skill from my mother, like pattern cutting, as a backup. I'd learn the software my first firm uses, because it will be the way the job's done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but steady. It feels like building a house and watching the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with five years that you couldn't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother says I should have a stable job and a craft as well, because crafts don't leave you. She'd also tell me not to worry about marriage for now, which is her way of showing she understands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mother want you to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work and also family. I'd want a husband one day and children, and I'd want to be able to feed them. Two years would make that feel impossible, but five years makes me think it can be done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing if people use it well, with hard work and good habits. I'd tell young people to learn a skill, save, and keep faith with their families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fairly settled. I'd have my qualification, a few years in a good firm, and the loan mostly gone. I'd also expect to be married, perhaps with a child, and a proper home, not a rented room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the exams, take a trainee job, and slowly learn the new tools as the firm brings them in. I'd pay off the loan in eight years and save for a deposit. I'd also help my mother with her business and keep a craft in the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a measure of hope. The faith helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a younger cousin about education and work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a skill that people need, a real one, not just a certificate. Accounting is good, but being useful to a neighbour is better. Don't borrow too much, and don't be too proud to ask your uncle for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still worry you with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the big companies would gain and the rest of us would be told to cope. Ten years is long enough for communities to build their own businesses, but we'd have to do it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2-year one, because I'd have no time to earn my way, only a big debt and a degree for the wrong decade. What would help is community support, a way into apprenticeships and the state as a backstop for food and rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what keeps me steady. It's my faith and my mother's sewing machine. I hear my mother's sewing machine at night through the wall, and it reminds me that honest work never stops.

headlineQuote: I hear my mother's sewing machine at night through the wall, and it reminds me that honest work never stops.
portrait: Jade is a **24-year-old** accounting master's student in Leicester with a 39,000 pound loan, an average result and no internship.
She is **traditional**: values earning, apprenticeships, family and faith, and sees the state as a last backstop.
She is **resistant** to AI and will learn software only when a firm shows her.
Her mood is **alarmed** for most worlds because entry-level accounting work looks exposed and no one can vouch for her.
Her mother's **sewing work** gives her a craft fallback and a family model of honest work.
biggestWorry: Jade fears **2028** most, because she would have no time to earn her way, only debt.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **community support**, a way into apprenticeships and the state as a last backstop.
